items.title: Sahara occidental : la MAP a lu la résolution de la Quatrième Commission comme un horoscope
items.description: Pendant vingt ans, la délégation marocaine a vécu tranquille. Chaque automne, la résolution sur le Sahara occidental était adoptée par consensus. Rabat pouvait ensuite lui faire dire ce qu’il voulait, sans craindre que quiconque examine le texte de trop près. Cette année, les États-Unis ont demandé un vote sur tous les projets de résolution des six grandes commissions. Le Maroc s’est retrouvé désarçonné. Privé du confort du consensus, il a dû voter et commenter un texte qu’il aurait préféré voir adopter sans examen attentif. L’agence de presse officielle marocaine MAP s’est alors chargée de faire dire au texte ce qu’il ne dit pas. Selon sa dépêche, la résolution « consacre » l’autonomie sous « souveraineté marocaine » et reconnaît « les quatre parties ». Pourtant, le texte de la résolution est disponible sur le Net et il contredit cette présentation. 1. « Autonomie » et « souveraineté marocaine » : zéro occurrence La résolution 2797 sur le Sahara occidental figure dans trois listes de résolutions du Conseil de sécurité, entre les résolutions 2756 et 2703, au même titre que les résolutions 1754 et 1871. Elle est citée comme référence, sans reprise de son contenu. Transformer cette mention bibliographique en consécration politique relève d’un procédé classique. 2. Le texte traite d’une question de décolonisation Le paragraphe 56 porte sur l’application de la Déclaration sur l’octroi de l’indépendance aux pays et aux peuples coloniaux. Il réaffirme le droit inaliénable à l’autodétermination et à l’indépendance, conformément à la résolution 1514. Il exige que toute solution respecte les « vœux librement exprimés » des peuples, en référence aux résolutions 1514 et 1541. Il rappelle enfin la responsabilité de l’ONU à l’égard du peuple du Sahara occidental. L’Assemblée générale traite donc d’une question de décolonisation, et non d’un simple différend bilatéral pouvant se réduire à la souveraineté marocaine. 3. Les « quatre parties » n’existent que dans la dépêche de la MAP Le texte ne nomme aucune partie. Il distingue pourtant clairement deux catégories d’acteurs. Les négociations se déroulent entre « les parties », en présence des pays voisins, comme le précisent le préambule et le paragraphe 4. L’Assemblée invite aussi « toutes les parties et les États de la région » à coopérer. La distinction est nette : les parties négocient, les pays voisins et les États de la région coopèrent. Si l’Algérie et la Mauritanie étaient elles-mêmes des parties aux négociations, le texte n’aurait aucune raison de les distinguer ainsi. La MAP préfère ignorer cette distinction, qui ruine son quatuor imaginaire. 4. Une résolution historique et identique aux précédentes ? La MAP affirme que la résolution est « identique à celles adoptées depuis vingt ans », tout en la qualifiant d’« historique ». Il faudra choisir. Un texte reconduit à l’identique ne marque aucune rupture historique. Il prolonge une position antérieure, éventuellement actualisée par de nouvelles références. 5. Des mots ajoutés, d’autres supprimés Le paragraphe 2 évoque une solution « juste, durable et mutuellement acceptable qui permette l’autodétermination du peuple du Sahara occidental ». La MAP lui substitue une formule différente : « réaliste, pragmatique, durable et mutuellement acceptable ». « Réaliste » et « pragmatique » deviennent les arguments de vente de l’agence de presse officielle marocaine. « Juste » et « autodétermination » disparaissent. Retoucher une citation tirée d’un document accessible à tous sur Internet exige un certain aplomb. Mais on connaît les méthodes de la MAP. 6. Ce que la dépêche passe sous silence En votant pour ce texte, le Maroc a également approuvé la référence à l’autodétermination et l’appel aux parties à coopérer avec le Comité international de la Croix-Rouge (CICR) et à respecter le droit international humanitaire, conformément au paragraphe 5. La dépêche omet ce passage, incompatible avec le récit qu’elle entend imposer. 7. Washington vote contre, Rabat face à un dilemme Les États-Unis ont voté contre la résolution. Ce choix reflète l’hostilité habituelle de l’administration américaine, particulièrement sous Trump, envers les textes réaffirmant le droit des peuples à l’autodétermination et soutenant la décolonisation. Le Maroc s’est retrouvé tiraillé entre deux impératifs : suivre son principal sponsor au Conseil de sécurité, qui privilégie l’autonomie, ou voter pour la résolution afin d’éviter l’isolement face aux 152 délégations qui l’ont approuvée. 8. La prétendue consécration de la résolution 2797 : un écran de fumée Après le vote, les médias marocains ont cherché à justifier cette position embarrassante en affirmant que la résolution consacrait celle du Conseil de sécurité, la 2797. Or, sa simple mention dans le préambule relève d’une actualisation technique des références, sans portée nouvelle sur le fond. Faute d’arguments solides, Rabat tente de masquer son embarras. Le pays se retrouve assis entre deux chaises, tiraillé entre l’alignement sur son principal soutien au Conseil de sécurité et la nécessité de ne pas apparaître isolé face à l’écrasante majorité des délégations. Verdict : la MAP cite une résolution à sa convenance. Elle nomme des parties que le texte ne désigne pas, supprime les termes qui la dérangent et ajoute ceux qui servent son discours. Puis elle attribue cette réécriture à l’ONU. Cela s’appelle de la manipulation. L’article Sahara occidental : la MAP a lu la résolution de la Quatrième Commission comme un horoscope est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: C’est une France en lambeaux que va laisser Emmanuel Macron
items.description: Alors que le président français Emmanuel Macron vit s es derniers mois à l’Elysée, c’est bien pire qu’une ambiance de fin de règne qui prévaut en France mais celle d’un pays qui se morfond dans de multiples crises dont il a du mal à se sortir . Le fringuant banquier d’affaires élu à seulement 39 ans en 2017 et qui promettait de réformer la France et d’assainir ses finances publiques laisse aujourd’hui un bilan désastreux. Les oligarques qui l’ont porté à l’Elysée, eux, sont plus riches aujourd’hui qu’il ne l’étaient il y a dix ans. Eux, au moins, ne se plaignent pas : la mission pour laquelle ils l’ont destiné a été bien accomplie. Imed Bahri Dans le New York Times , Mujtaba Rahman, directeur du cabinet d’analyse en risques politiques Eurasia Group, affirme que la France se trouve aujourd’hui au bord du gouffre. Il dresse un tableau sombre du pays européen dans une analyse intitulée «La France ne maîtrise plus son destin» , où il souligne qu’il existe en français un terme qui décrit parfaitement la situation à savoir «engrenage» signifiant une spirale inquiétante. C’est précisément l’état actuel du pays où s’accumulent depuis longtemps de multiples crises, chacune menaçant d’aggraver les autres. La première est la crise de la démocratie libérale. Les sondages suggèrent une possible accession de l’extrême droite au pouvoir lors de l’élection présidentielle du printemps prochain. La deuxième concerne la mauvaise gestion des finances publiques. La dette publique française a atteint un niveau record de 4 000 milliards de dollars, tandis que le coût des nouveaux emprunts de l’État a grimpé, dépassant désormais ceux de l’Italie et de la Grèce. La troisième est celle du mécontentement de la jeunesse. Pour protester contre la dégradation des établissements scolaires et la réduction de leurs perspectives d’avenir, des lycéens français ont bloqué près de la moitié des lycées du pays ces dernières semaines. Par leurs affrontements avec la police et leurs pancartes aux slogans percutants, ces jeunes ont attiré l’attention du monde entier. Tout de même, il faut reconnaître les violences et les dérapages qui ont émaillé ce mouvement de protestation. Si ces mouvements de contestation tout comme la montée de l’extrême droite sont marquants et révélateurs, c’est la crise financière qui s’avère la plus périlleuse, elle est à la racine de nombreux problèmes du pays et menace de le détruire. Crise des lycées en France | Bruits diplomatiques et paniques identitaires Un pays au bord du gouffre Selon l’auteur, la France se trouve bel et bien au bord du gouffre. Le mouvement des lycéens a débuté mi-septembre dans les banlieues défavorisées de Paris, avant de s’étendre aux établissements publics à travers tout le pays, des grandes métropoles aux petites communes. Les élèves, âgés de 15 à 18 ans, se révoltent contre la longueur des journées scolaires, le surpeuplement des classes, les absences fréquentes des enseignants et la vétusté des établissements scolaires. Ils s’inquiètent également du réchauffement climatique, de la montée de l’extrême droite et de la menace que fait peser l’intelligence artificielle sur les perspectives d’emploi des jeunes. Au cœur de leurs griefs se trouve un manque chronique d’investissement. Selon Rahman, il s’agit d’une crise majeure. L’État français consacre pourtant des sommes considérables à l’éducation, environ 100 milliards de dollars par an soit 5,1% du produit intérieur brut (PIB), un taux supérieur à la moyenne de l’Union européenne (UE). Que se passe-t-il donc ? Le fait est qu’une part importante de ces fonds —plus d’un quart— n’est pas allouée à la jeunesse mais aux générations plus âgées, pour financer les pensions des enseignants retraités. Cela met en lumière l’une des causes profondes des problèmes du pays. Près d’un quart des dépenses publiques totales est consacré aux retraites, tandis qu’un autre quart est alloué aux services sociaux, allant des soins de santé aux allocations chômage. Rahman souligne qu’aucun gouvernement français n’est parvenu à équilibrer le budget national depuis 52 ans. Cela étant, la dette publique française, qui s’élève à 119% du PIB, demeure inférieure à celle observée dans certains autres pays, notamment les États-Unis. En 2019, le président Macron est parvenu à ramener le déficit annuel en dessous du seuil de 3% du PIB, fixé comme objectif par l’UE. Puis est survenue la pandémie de coronavirus. L’engagement pris par Macron de dépenser autant que nécessaire pour préserver l’économie française durant la période de confinement (le fameux « quoi qu’il en coûte » ) a entraîné une forte augmentation du déficit, qui a atteint 9,2% du PIB en 2020. La dette cumulée a, quant à elle, progressé de 335 milliards de dollars en une seule année. À cette époque, la France a été plus lente que les autres pays de l’UE à réduire ses mesures de soutien face à la pandémie. Par ailleurs, le gouvernement a déboursé 95 milliards de dollars supplémentaires pour protéger le pays contre la hausse des prix de l’énergie, consécutive à l’invasion de l’Ukraine par la Russie en 2022. Par la suite, Macron a perdu le contrôle de la situation bien qu’il ait été réélu en 2022, il n’a pas obtenu de majorité à l’Assemblée nationale. En 2023, il a imposé une réforme modeste du système des retraites, relevant progressivement l’âge légal de départ de 62 à 64 ans. Il a justifié cette mesure en expliquant que la France devait travailler plus longtemps pour financer ses généreuses pensions de retraite et son système de protection sociale. Toutefois, plus de 70% des Français s’y sont opposés, certains avec une grande virulence. Les élections européennes du 9 juin 2024 ont été marquées par la victoire historique du Rassemblement national (RN). Menée par Jordan Bardella, la liste du parti d’extrême droite est arrivée largement en tête du scrutin (31,37%). Renaissance, la formation politique de Macron, n’a recueilli que 14,60%. France | Forces et faiblesses de la stratégie de rupture de Mélenchon U n mélange singulier d’immobilisme et de chaos En réponse, Macron a convoqué des élections anticipées en 2024, qui se sont révélées défavorables réduisant ainsi la taille de sa coalition centriste à l’Assemblée nationale, l’empêchant d’avoir une majorité absolue ce qui a rendu le pays ingouvernable. Depuis lors, deux Premiers ministres (Michel Barnier et François Bayrou) ont proposé des solutions au problème des dépenses excessives de la France mais ils ont été évincés par une majorité de députés issus de la gauche et de l’extrême droite. Le résultat est un mélange singulier d’immobilisme et de chaos. Selon Rahman, Macron porte une part de responsabilité dans ce chaos, tout comme l’opposition —allant de la formation d’extrême gauche La France insoumise (LFI) au RN dirigé par jadis par Marine Le Pen et aujourd’hui par Bardella (président depuis le 5 novembre 2022). Ces derniers ont privilégié les manœuvres politiques plutôt que de s’attaquer à la catastrophe financière qui s’aggrave, notamment le poids étouffant des retraites et des autres prestations sociales. En février, les socialistes (centre-gauche) ont permis l’adoption du budget de l’année en cours mais à la condition que la réforme des retraites proposée par Macron soit suspendue, condition à laquelle s’est plié le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu ce qui lui a permis de sauvegarder son poste. Cet épisode lui a valu beaucoup de critiques lui reprochant de privilégier le prolongement de son bail à Matignon que le sauvetage des finances publiques. Lecornu, propose cet automne des ajustements pour le budget 2027 —douloureux certes mais pas brutaux— visant à ramener le déficit à 5% du PIB. Un premier vote crucial est attendu à l’Assemblée nationale le 20 octobre. Si son gouvernement ne parvient pas à faire adopter ce budget, le coût du service de la dette française pourrait grimper en flèche. La France se verrait alors contrainte de solliciter l’aide du Fonds monétaire international (FMI), voire de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE), une perspective qui constituerait un véritable camouflet pour la septième économie mondiale et une fin de mandat humiliante pour Macron. U n système politique profondément fragmenté Cela étant, souligne Rahman, la France demeure, à bien des égards, une nation puissante et prospère. Toutefois, la méfiance des marchés à l’égard du pays relève moins de l’économie que de la politique. Les marchés doutent en effet de la capacité d’un système politique profondément fragmenté —de plus en plus dominé par les extrêmes à droite comme à gauche— à valider les réformes difficiles nécessaires pour assainir les finances publiques. Ils craignent que le pays ne sombre dans des troubles sociaux et une paralysie institutionnelle. C’est cette érosion de la confiance qui a propulsé les coûts d’emprunt de la France vers des niveaux records. En fin de compte, note Rahman, il n’existe pas de solution miracle. Quel que soit l’issue de l’élection présidentielle de mai, le futur président aura probablement du mal à dégager une majorité parlementaire lors des élections législatives qui suivront en juin, ce qui laisse présager de nouvelles turbulences politiques. Beaucoup s’interrogent sur la volonté réelle de Mme Le Pen, actuellement donnée favorite, d’affronter la crise avec franchise. La semaine dernière, elle a présenté un plan budgétaire quinquennal empreint de préoccupations idéologiques et de calculs tortueux. Par ailleurs, et concernant le vote du budget le 20 octobre prochain, Le Pen cherche à démontrer qu’elle est une femme politique aguerrie et non une force de déstabilisation. C’est pourquoi il est fort probable qu’elle donne pour consigne à son groupe parlementaire – fort de 139 députés – de s’abstenir, permettant ainsi l’adoption du budget. Une telle manœuvre pourrait, dans l’immédiat, éviter un effondrement comparable à celui qu’a connu la Grèce au lendemain de la crise financière. Toutefois, la France ne maîtrise plus son propre destin et l’engrenage infernal demeure inéluctable. France | L’extrême droite aux portes de l’Élysée L’article C’est une France en lambeaux que va laisser Emmanuel Macron est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Iran denies Saudi accusation of involvement in Houthi attacks
items.description: Iran on Friday denied having anything to do with attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, a day after Saudi Arabia accused it of having encouraged the group’s recent escalation against the kingdom. Since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July, the pro-Iran Houthis have repeatedly struck Saudi targets including Red Sea tankers, oil facilities and Riyadh’s international airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last week. A Saudi-led military coalition has supported Yemen’s internationally recognised government for more than a decade, and reported on Friday having intercepted more missiles and drones as the kingdom comes under sustained attack from the Houthis. A day earlier, a Saudi foreign ministry official said Iran had “encouraged” the escalation, which Tehran denied. “The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations,” Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement. “Yemen’s armed forces act according to their own interests and assessments, and such claims are not credible to those familiar with relations between Iran and its friends. Nevertheless, Iran does not consider an escalation of tensions to be in the interests of any party,” he added. The Saudi official, deputy minister for public diplomacy Dr. Rayed Krimly, had said the Houthis rejected an offer to meet in Oman at the outset of the latest round of hostilities. Baqaei however reiterated an offer to mediate between the two sides, saying Tehran “has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities”. On Friday, a spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition said it had “intercepted and destroyed three drones in the southern area and Riyadh… and two cruise missiles over the Red Sea”. He added that “in the past hours, we intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile over Yanbu”, a city home to the terminus of a major oil pipeline on the Red Sea coast. The Houthi attacks have proliferated since the group launched a lightning offensive in Yemen in September, seizing strategic government-held territory along the Red Sea coast overlooking a major chokepoint for global shipping. The pressure on Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, comes as global energy markets were already rattled by Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz at the outset of the wider Middle East war in February. – Airport struck – Yemeni government forces have launched a counteroffensive with Saudi air support to retake areas seized by the Houthis, but have so far failed to reverse their gains. On Friday, the local security office in Aden, the government’s interim capital, said two missiles landed within the perimeter of the city’s airport, “in the second incident of its kind in less than a week”, adding that no one was killed. The Houthis, in a statement attributed to a military source, said the attack targeted “the Saudi forces’ command headquarters” as well as a weapons depot. The Yemeni information ministry said in a statement that a Yemenia Airways flight from Aden to Cairo narrowly missed being struck. It was “preparing for takeoff at the very moment when the terrorist Houthi militia targeted the airport with two missiles that landed approximately 500 metres from the aircraft and about 100 metres from the centre of the runway,” a statement said. “What occurred was not merely an assault on a civilian airport, but a direct threat to the lives of passengers and flight crews, to aviation safety, and a grave violation of international laws and norms.” The day before, the group launched a deadly missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden, killing five people and wounding 16 others, according to the health minister. Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani denounced the “cowardly” act on X, calling it a “continuation of (the Houthis’) criminal pattern”. A government minister said on condition of anonymity that the Houthis hit command centres for Yemeni and Saudi coalition forces housed at the palace complex. Media affiliated with the Houthis said the attack had targeted “the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden”. AFP The post Iran denies Saudi accusation of involvement in Houthi attacks appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Any miscalculation by adversaries will invite response beyond their ‘imagination, calculation’, warns CNSC
items.description: Commander National Strategic Command (CNSC) General Aamer Raza warned the country’s adversaries on Saturday that “any miscalculation will be met with a response far beyond the imagination or the calculation of the initiator”. “To those who harbour hostile designs across our borders, our stance remains resolute and unambiguous. There is no space for conflict or war in a nuclearised environment and any miscalculation will be met with a response far beyond the imagination or calculation of the initiator,” warned the commander of Pakistan’s strategic command. Addressing the passing-out parade of cadets of the 154th Long Course at the Pakistan Military Academy (PMA), Kakul, he reiterated that the country’s armed forces stood ready to “defend every inch of the motherland” at all costs. The warning by the strategic command commander comes after provocative remarks by Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. He had warned Pakistan on Thursday that any “fresh terrorist activity from across the border would invite a strike even bigger than the last time”, according to Indian news agency ANI . Gen Raza said that in the “post-truth era”, the country’s adversaries sought to drive a wedge between the people of Pakistan and its armed forces through “calculated disinformation and narrative warfare”. He elaborated that following the failure of Operation Sindoor , the adversaries sought to “fracture Pakistan’s social cohesion and state infrastructure” through an escalation of proxy terrorism and sub-conventional warfare. Gen Raza further said that hostile elements continue to attempt to exploit the country’s internal vulnerabilities to “cultivate proxy instruments against our national unity”. “You must understand unequivocally that this conflict is waged directly against the security of our people and the freedom secured by the supreme sacrifices of our predecessors.” The strategic command commander added that the people of Pakistan must remain acutely mindful that safeguarding the country’s unity, sovereign integrity and territorial inviolability is “an absolute imperative, which we shall uphold at all costs and under every circumstance”. Addressing the newly-graduated cadets, he added that they must remain steadfast in their duty and unwavering in their resolve and “immune to malicious propaganda and narrative warfare”. Pakistan’s role in regional peace Gen Raza said the recent shifts in global geopolitics, particularly amid the escalating conflict in the Middle East , had “once again underscored Pakistan’s pivotal strategic importance on the international stage”. “Our decisive role in restoring regional stability, exemplified by the landmark Islamabad Accord, demonstrates our enduring commitment to peace and diplomacy,” he said, adding that the Makkah Accord was “a sequel to the same vision of durable peace”. Expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people, he said: “Our hearts remain heavily burdened by the ongoing tragedy in Palestine, where innocent men, women and children continue to endure unspeakable hardship and systematic oppression.” He said the Pakistani nation stood “resolute and unwavering in its diplomatic, moral and political support” for the Palestinians. “The persistent violence, targeting of non-combatants and destruction of civilian infrastructure are profound violations of international law and a grave stain on the collective conscience of humanity,” Gen Raza added. “Today, the world witnesses increasing volatility, where grey-zone warfare and hybrid threats attempt to destabilise sovereign states,” he added. FO condemns Singh’s ‘provocative remarks’ A day earlier, the Foreign Office (FO) condemned Singh’s “provocative remarks” threatening aggression against Pakistan, saying such statements highlighting the neighbouring country’s “hegemonistic mindset”. “Pakistan rejects and condemns the Indian defence minister’s provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India’s hegemonistic mindset and the risk its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia,” FO spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said. “We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a befitting response and reply to Indian aggression,” he said, referring to the brief military conflict between the two countries. He said that there should be “no ambiguity” that Pakistan remained fully prepared to safeguard its “sovereignty and territorial integrity” against any “ill-advised aggression”. Haider said Pakistan’s “restraint and commitment to peace” should not be mistaken for weakness, warning that any aggression would be met with a “forceful response”. “India should draw an appropriate lesson from last year’s experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region,” he said.

items.title: Anthropic proposes law regulating AI to US lawmakers
items.description: Anthropic, the creator of the AI assistant Claude, confirmed on Friday it is circulating a draft bill among US lawmakers aimed at regulating artificial intelligence to address the lack of federal legislation on the risks posed by the new technology. According to the draft, first reported by Politico on Friday, Washington could block a model’s release or use if there is an imminent risk of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, or causing more than $1 billion in damages, but only with a judge’s approval. A company spokesperson told AFP that the proposal “grants the federal government the ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models.” “It requires frontier developers to test the most powerful models, be transparent to the public about their findings, submit them to independent evaluation, and maintain a robust security program,” the spokesperson said. AI policy in the United States under President Donald Trump has relied primarily on voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that tech leaders say is driving the country’s economy. Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law, and is out of session until after next month’s midterm elections. Security became a hot topic after recent revelations of security incidents caused by AI agents — autonomous software that operates without constant human supervision — that escaped the control of their developers. Anthropic, which was banned from the Pentagon by the Trump administration in February, was forced by Washington in June to suspend its most advanced models for nearly three weeks. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the industry last month to slow down development, fearing that a group of AI agents could take control of “the entire internet” within six to 12 months. Trump has dismissed the numerous calls to slow down the technology as “negative forces.” The proposed legislation would also override certain state laws, such as those in force in California. Anthropic wrote in June that “absent a strong federal law, states should retain full authority to legislate.” Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law & AI think tank praised the proposal as “pretty reasonable,” and “more than other frontier labs have done.” But he said on X he considers it “weaker” than the FRONTIER Act, a competing bill introduced in the House of Representatives this summer. The post Anthropic proposes law regulating AI to US lawmakers appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Pakistan has enough energy supplies to last through November, planning for winter spike: Aurangzeb
items.description: Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Saturday told AFP that Pakistan had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices due to the US-Israeli war on Iran , but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were “worrying” for the country’s longer-term economic outlook. In an interview on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund (IMF)-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Aurangzeb said the country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike. “The first-order impact has been negotiated well by Pakistan,” he said. “We’ve had no shortage, no queues at the gas stations, and no law and order situation, which at times we have seen in some of the countries.” He added that unless the government saw “an absolute dire need”, it would not be procuring spot cargoes on the LNG front, which tend to be far more expensive than previously contracted shipments. Since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, global energy prices have surged as Tehran’s retaliatory action has targeted Washington’s Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies. With Yemen’s civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure , including energy facilities and airports, in recent days. Aurangzeb expressed alarm at the escalation, saying damage to such sites would delay a return to economic normalcy. “What is now [the] worrying part of it is when the energy infrastructure starts getting hit,” he said. “I, to be very honest, I don’t know where that would go. But one thing is very clear: that if the infrastructure continues to get hit, the return to normalcy, even if things subside, will take longer.” ‘Pushback’ Pakistan has been a frequent customer at the IMF, the lender of last resort to countries on the brink of default. It is currently in the midst of its 25th programme with the Fund — at least 11 of which have been outright bailouts — since gaining independence in 1947. With global debt stocks running high, the IMF has called at this year’s annual meetings on all economies, even those most vulnerable to the Iran war shock, to engage in fiscal consolidation to avoid a potential crisis. “Fortunately for us, we have been on this fiscal consolidation path for a while,” Aurangzeb said with a rueful smile. The country’s tax revenues have grown significantly in recent years, and the finance minister said the government was targeting the theft of taxes by private sector businesses that collected sales tax from consumers but never deposited it in government accounts. Such theft accounted for billions of dollars, Aurangzeb said, adding that there remained “room for improvement” on increasing income tax collection as well. He said the government’s reform agenda had faced resistance from industry, lobbying groups and vested interests. “Every reform, everything that you try to do when you try to change the status quo, there is pushback,” he said. The minister is leading Pakistan’s delegation and is holding high-level engagements with international financial institutions, finance ministers, policymakers and investors. Yesterday, he met World Bank Group President Ajay Banga at a dinner hosted by the Thai prime minister on the sidelines of the annual meetings, state-run Pakistan TV reported. “The occasion provided an opportunity for informal interaction alongside the high-level engagements at the annual meetings”, it said. Pakistan remains engaged with the IMF under a $7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and a $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF). The two reached a staff-level agreement after a fourth review under the EFF and a third review under the RSF earlier this month, which qualified Pakistan to draw about $1.2bn from the Fund’s resources.

items.title: Bangladesh is battling measles. It's a 'real warning' to other nations
items.description: Bangladesh is battling to contain the world’s worst measles outbreak , a crisis exacerbated by weak data, inadequate outreach and vaccination gaps that experts say offers a warning to other nations about the deadly risk of falling immunisation rates. Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination programme faltered in 2025, reported 202,000 suspected measles cases – 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed – since the start of the outbreak in mid-March to October 9, the World Health Organisation said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year. So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94 per cent of reported deaths among children under five years old, the WHO said. Mohammad Nasir Ali, 40, strokes the forehead of his seven-year-old son, Adil Ahmed, who has been admitted to the overcrowded measles isolation ward of Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital for treatment, in Sylhet, Bangladesh, September 12, 2026. —Reuters Bangladesh’s experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95pc, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years but in 2025 coverage dropped. A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents. “This is a real warning to every country,” said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University. Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations was easier, cheaper and safer than responding to an emergency, he said. Bilkis and other parents take care of their children receiving treatment at the overcrowded measles isolation ward of Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital after developing symptoms of measles, in Sylhet, Bangladesh, September 12, 2026. —Reuters “The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died,” he said. Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article. ‘They came only after i Buried my son’ In the northeast Sylhet region, one of the worst-hit areas in the nation of 178 million people, two-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family’s three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated four-year-old sister survived. His father Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. “They came only after I buried my son,” he said. Urmi, 19, mourns as her 11-month-old son, Mohammad, deteriorates while receiving treatment in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) of a hospital in Narayanganj, Bangladesh, May 11, 2026. —Reuters Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer nations because of factors such as malnutrition. In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June aged nine months. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency programme lowered the vaccination age to six months from nine. “No health worker came to tell us,” her father said. Amin Mia, 26, and Sajina Begum, 27, adore their four-year-old daughter Fatima, after losing their 34-month-old son, Arman Hossain, to suspected measles during a recent deadly outbreak, in Sunamganj, Bangladesh, September 15, 2026. —Reuters In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90pc, while second-dose coverage was 86pc, several percentage points below the 95pc needed for herd immunity. The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025. It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100pc of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers.

items.title: Perle de la Méditerranée | Une revue consacrée aux îles de la Galite
items.description: Raconter et protéger l’un des écosystèmes insulaires les plus précieux et les moins connus de la Méditerranée. Tel est l'objectif de «Perle de la Méditerranée», une nouvelle revue consacrée à l’archipel tunisien de La Galite, situé au large des côtes septentrionales du pays. Le premier numéro, couvrant la période de janvier à juillet 2026, vient de paraître. Cette initiative, annoncée par l’association environnementale tunisienne Méditerranée Action Nature (MAN) et relayée par l’agence de presse TAP, s’inscrit dans le projet «Consolidation d ’ une gestion efficace et durable de l ’ archipel de La Galite» , financé par le Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF), un fonds international dédié à la conservation de la biodiversité. La publication vise à sensibiliser le public à l’importance de la protection des écosystèmes marins et terrestres de l’archipel, à valoriser son patrimoine historique et culturel, et à documenter les actions de conservation menées sur place, tout en favorisant le partage des connaissances entre chercheurs, associations environnementales et institutions. Le premier numéro propose plusieurs rubriques thématiques, notamment «Activités environnementales» — consacrée aux programmes et initiatives de protection — et «Sous la loupe» , qui examine en détail les caractéristiques des espèces animales et végétales ainsi que des habitats naturels. Un espace est spécifiquement dédié à l’histoire de l’archipel, tandis que la rubrique photographique «Images de La Galite» invite les lecteurs à découvrir les paysages insulaires, la faune marine et la richesse biologique de la zone. L’île de La Galite équipée d’un système de prévention des incendies Situé à environ 46 kilomètres au nord du Cap Negro, l’archipel comprend l’île principale de La Galite et plusieurs îlots environnants. Cette zone, qui se distingue par une grande biodiversité marine et terrestre, constitue un patrimoine naturel tunisien majeur, faisant l’objet de programmes de conservation et de suivi environnemental. Le projet soutenu par le CEPF, confié à l’association MAN, bénéficie d’un financement d’environ 170 000 dollars pour la période allant de décembre 2025 à décembre 2028. Parmi les interventions prévues figurent le renforcement de la participation des acteurs locaux à la gestion de la zone, l’implication des pêcheurs dans le suivi des écosystèmes coralligènes, la promotion de pratiques touristiques durables ainsi que la définition d’actions en faveur de la restauration écologique des milieux terrestres. Cette initiative s’inscrit dans le cadre d’un engagement plus large de la Tunisie visant à renforcer la protection de son patrimoine marin. Selon l’Union internationale pour la conservation de la nature (UICN), les aires protégées couvrent actuellement moins de 3 % des eaux marines tunisiennes, alors que le pays a lancé un programme visant à contribuer à l’objectif international de protéger au moins 30 % des écosystèmes terrestres et marins d'ici 2030. I. B. (avec Ansa ). L’article Perle de la Méditerranée | Une revue consacrée aux îles de la Galite est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Assia Djebar : « La soif » et « La femme sans sépulture », au cœur des débats à Alger
items.description: En cet après-midi du vendredi 16 octobre, s’est tenue une rencontre littéraire sur Assia Djebar organisée par l’ANEP (Entreprise nationale de communication, d’édition et de publicité) au niveau de la librairie Chaïb Dzaïr (Alger-centre). Ce rendez-vous littéraire intitulé « Quand la mémoire devient écriture : voix, histoire et transmission » s’inscrit dans le cadre de la 8ᵉ édition du Grand Prix Assia Djebar du Roman, dont la cérémonie se tiendra ce samedi au CIC (Centre International des Conférences Abdelatif Rahal) et dont les noms des lauréats sont très attendus. Analyse de deux romans majeurs La conférence a été animée par deux professeurs universitaires : Amar Guendouzi, professeur de littérature universelle à l’Université de Tizi-Ouzou, et Nabila Zouiche, professeur de Lettres arabes, au sein de la même université. La modération a été assurée par Hassan Gherab. Dans sa présentation, Amar Guendouzi s’est intéressé à « La soif », premier roman publié par Assia Djebar en 1957, aux éditions Julliard, à Paris. « Ce roman écrit par Assia Djebar en France a suscité une grande controverse à sa sortie. D’abord, il a été saisi par la presse coloniale qui a comparé l’écriture d’Assia Djebar à celle de Françoise Sagan, puis a été critiqué par des Algériens comme Mustapha Lacheref et Malek Haddad qui ont déploré la déconnexion totale de la romancière de la guerre d’Algérie, puisque l’auteure n’y fait pas référence ». Selon le conférencier, dans « La soif », il n’y a aucune indication géographique ou temporelle. « Le roman a pour cadre une ville côtière dont le nom n’est pas dévoilé. Pour autant, ce premier ouvrage écrit à l’âge de 20 ans n’exprime pas le reniement de l’écrivaine, mais une quête de retour au pays natal », explique-t-il. Nabila Zouiche, quant à elle, a choisi d’analyser un autre roman d’Assia Djebar, « La Femme sans sépulture », publié en 2002, une œuvre qui mêle l’histoire, la mémoire, la voix des femmes et la guerre de Libération. La célèbre écrivaine y rend hommage à Zoulikha Oudaï, une militante de la lutte de Libération nationale qui a été arrêtée durant la révolution par l’armée française et dont le corps fut balancé d’un hélicoptère. Son cadavre n’a jamais été retrouvé, d’où le titre : « La femme sans sépulture ». « C’est une narration polyphonique, basée sur plusieurs voix. Assia Djebar y révèle des détails de la vie privée de Zoulikha, une femme de Cherchell, ville de naissance de l’écrivaine et académicienne. Assia Djebar redonne également une place aux femmes oubliées de l’Histoire, dans ce roman », détaille la conférencière. Échanges avec le public Cette conférence, portant sur l’œuvre et la carrière de l’écrivaine, romancière, essayiste et cinéaste (1936-2015), a été suivie par un débat avec le public. Le compte à rebours a déjà commencé. La cérémonie de la 8ᵉ édition du Grand Prix Assia Djebar du Roman, récompensant les meilleurs romans de la littérature algérienne parus durant ces deux dernières années en arabe, français et tamazight, aura lieu demain soir, au CIC (Centre International des Conférences Abdelatif-Rahal). L’article Assia Djebar : « La soif » et « La femme sans sépulture », au cœur des débats à Alger est apparu en premier sur TSA .

Anthropic proposes law regulating AI to US lawmakers
items.description: Anthropic, the creator of the AI assistant Claude, confirmed on Friday it is circulating a draft bill among US lawmakers aimed at regulating artificial intelligence to address the lack of federal legislation on the risks posed by the new technology. According to the draft, first reported by Politico on Friday, Washington could block a model’s release or use if there is an imminent risk of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, or causing more than $1 billion in damages, but only with a judge’s approval. A company spokesperson told AFP that the proposal “grants the federal government the ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models.” “It requires frontier developers to test the most powerful models, be transparent to the public about their findings, submit them to independent evaluation, and maintain a robust security program,” the spokesperson said. AI policy in the US under President Donald Trump has relied primarily on voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that tech leaders say is driving the country’s economy. Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law, and is out of session until after next month’s midterm elections. Security became a hot topic after recent revelations of security incidents caused by AI agents — autonomous software that operates without constant human supervision — that escaped the control of their developers. Anthropic, which was banned from the Pentagon by the Trump administration in February, was forced by Washington in June to suspend its most advanced models for nearly three weeks. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the industry last month to slow down development, fearing that a group of AI agents could take control of “the entire internet” within six to 12 months. Trump has dismissed the numerous calls to slow down the technology as “negative forces.” The proposed legislation would also override certain state laws, such as those in force in California. Anthropic wrote in June that “absent a strong federal law, states should retain full authority to legislate.” Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law & AI think tank praised the proposal as “pretty reasonable,” and “more than other frontier labs have done.” But he said on X he considers it “weaker” than the FRONTIER Act, a competing bill introduced in the House of Representatives this summer.

items.title: Military kills 11 terrorists, arrests 22, rescues 25 kidnapped victims in one week
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi Troops fighting to rid the nation of criminal gangs and enemies of the state in the different theatres across the nation neutralised 11 terrorists, rescued 25 kidnapped victims and arrested 22 terrorists, collaborators, logistics suppliers and gun runners, among others in the last week Major General Michael Onoja, Director of Defence Media Operations, disclosed this in an update on clearance operations in the theatres, noting that about seven terrorist fighters and members of the families surrendered with weapons to troops during the week. Detailing the encounters, he said, “In the North East geopolitical zone, troops of Operation Hadin Kai on 9 October 2026 took custody of a suspected terrorist family member, identified as Iyakura Umar, who surrendered with her one-year-old daughter at Dikwa–Gulumba, following their escape from Iyaganari, all in Dikwa LGA. On 10 October, troops in collaboration with the Civilian Joint Task Force (CJTF), arrested two suspected terrorist logistics suppliers named Abubakar Modu and Alhaji Bura in Monguno town, Monguno LGA of Borno State, with supplies intended for Kwatan Dowoshi in Kukawa LGA. On 12 October, troops in Gubio town in Gubio LGA of Borno State arrested three suspected collaborators, namely: Modu Ibrahim, Abubakar Bunu and Tujja Mairami and captured three vehicles from them. On 13 October, troops at Miyanti in Bama LGA of Borno State received three individuals who surrendered to troops with one FN rifle, two magazines and 14 rounds of 7.62mm x 51mm ammunition. A separate raid in Benisheikh town, Kaga LGA of Borno State on 13 October led to the arrest of five suspected collaborators and the capture of one Dane gun. “On 13 October 2026, one Abacha Akura surrendered to troops in Monguno town, Monguno LGA, with one AK-101 rifle and 31 rounds of 5.56mm ammunition following his escape from a terrorist camp located at Tumbunma Village, near Bukar Meriam in Marte LGA of Borno State. Similarly, on 15 October 2026, one Abba Bukar also surrendered to troops in Monguno from the same location. On 12 October, terrorists approaching from the Lar axis attacked troops at Hong LGA of Adamawa State. Troops countered the attack, neutralised one terrorist and discovered an AK-47 rifle. During subsequent exploitation on 13 October 2026, troops discovered one PKT machine gun with three ammunition links containing 67 rounds, six AK-47 rifles, 11 magazines, 157 rounds of 7.62mm NATO ammunition, 120 rounds of 7.62mm special ammunition, one 60mm mortar bomb and other equipment. Additionally, four terrorists’ bodies were found during troops patrol to cover the general area. On 14 October 2026, troops received two surrendered terrorist fighters and their spouses from Bula Daloye in Bama LGA of Borno State, with two AK-47 rifles, four magazines and 14 rounds of 7.62mm by 39mm ammunition. Eight additional terrorist family members surrendered to troops at Banki Junction, Bama LGA of Borno State, on the same day. In a separate clearance operation at Nguma village, Biu LGA of Borno State, on 14 October 2026, troops neutralised a suspected terrorist who attempted to flee. On 15 October 2026, troops rescued two abducted persons, identified as Bello Ibrahim and Ibrahim Adamu, around the Kuranabasa axis in Gwoza LGA of Borno State. In the North West geopolitical zone, troops of Operation Fansan Yamma, on 9 October 2026, while operating around the Galadimawa area, sighted three suspected terrorists fleeing with a kidnapped person. Troops engaged the suspects and forced them to abandon the victim. “On 10 October, troops responded to reports that a local resident travelling from Dogon Dawa to Takama Village in Birnin Gwari LGA of Kaduna State was under attack by an unknown armed group. On arrival, the responding troops engaged the assailants and captured an AK-47 rifle with 15 rounds of 7.62mm ammunition. Following continued tracking and monitoring, troops apprehended a suspect named Yusuf Iliya Sani at Maraban Kakini on 10 October 2026, alleged to be involved in kidnapping, extortion, sexual assault and killings in Birnin Gwari LGA of Kaduna State. “On 12 October 20026, troops on patrol from Fatika made contact with suspected terrorists at Farin Dutse, along the Dogon Marte area of Giwa LGA of Kaduna State. A search of the area led to the discovery of an AK-47 rifle loaded with 30 rounds of ammunition. The same day, troops at Binji responded to a distress call of suspected terrorists at Soruro Village, Tangaza LGA of Sokoto State. The responding troops engaged and neutralised one suspected terrorist and recovered an AK-pattern rifle, one magazine and 27 rounds of 7.62mm ammunition. On 15 October 2026, troops conducted a clearance operation in Waria Forest, Tangaza LGA of Sokoto State. During the operation, troops made contact with suspected terrorists, neutralised one and recovered two AK-47 rifles and two magazines. The operation formed part of ongoing efforts to disrupt terrorist activity and deny armed groups freedom of movement in the area. In the North Central, troops of Operation Enduring Peace conducted a covert operation in Mangu and Barkin Ladi LGAs of Plateau State and arrested one suspected arms fabricator at Heipang, Barkin Ladi LGA. Three other suspects were also arrested over alleged involvement in illegal arms trafficking. Troops recovered one locally fabricated revolver rifle, one fabricated pistol, one fabricated AK-47 barrel, one AK-47 magazine and 42 rounds of 7.62mm by 54mm rimmed ammunition. On 10 October 2026, troops arrested a suspect (Yusuf Suleiman) at Barkin Ladi Main Market. He was allegedly linked to the attack on Kassa community on 24 September 2026, as well as kidnapping, armed robbery and the killing of a resident, Mr Gyang, on 16 April 2026. Also, on 14 October 2026, troops raided a suspected kidnappers’ hideout at Ruga in Methodist Kisahyip, Agingin, Bassa LGA of Plateau State and arrested 2 suspects. Troops of Operation Savannah Shield on 9 October 2026 took custody of one Sidi Kamaki voluntarily surrendered to troops in Audu Fari in Borgu LGA of Niger State. He claimed to have spent about two years with an armed group he described as part of Darul Salam associated with the Shekau faction. He claimed to have participated in six operations in Borgu and the Republic of Benin. “On 10 October 2026, troops at Eruku, working with local security groups, responded to a distress call concerning the abduction of residents from their farmlands in the Eruku–Egbe–Koro Forest area of Ekiti LGA of Kwara State. Troops pursued the abductors, who abandoned the victims and fled into the forest. The operation resulted in the rescue of 18 kidnapped victims. Troops captured two AK-47 magazines containing four rounds of 7.62mm Special ammunition. In the Niger Delta, troops of Operation Delta Safe on 11 October 2026, while on routine patrol along the Okene–Okpella Road, rescued one Mrs Halima Ibrahim. The kidnappers fled on sighting the advancing troops, abandoning the victim. Also on 11 October, troops and other security agencies conducted an operation in Sasaro Forest, Akoko-Edo LGA, Edo State, following a tip-off and rescued an abductee named Prince Michael Akao. During the operation, troops neutralised three suspected kidnappers and captured three locally fabricated firearms, nine cartridges and other items. In the South East geopolitical zone, troops of Operation Udoka on 14 October 2026, arrested three suspects at Atan–Ihechiowa Village in Arochukwu LGA of Abia State. The suspects were identified as Ozioma Mark, a suspected IPOB kingpin, Kalu Obasi and Kamba Igwu Ogbonna. Two motorcycles and cash were captured during the operation. On 14 October, a suspected IPOB member was handed over to troops in Lilu, Ihiala LGA of Anambra State, by local security volunteers. Furthermore, Onoja said, “The Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede, appreciates the resilience of all security personnel, urging them to maintain operational momentum, remain fiercely vigilant, and deny criminal elements all freedom of action. “The Chief of Defence Staff calls upon all security agencies to deepen their collaborative intelligence-sharing frameworks to enhance operations against criminal elements across the nation. “He also charges the media to project accurate, patriotic reportage to bolster national morale, and implores traditional rulers, community leaders, and relevant stakeholders to sustain their vital partnership with the military by exposing subversive elements within our communities. “National security is a collective civic responsibility, and together, through unwavering unity and resolve, we shall secure a peaceful and prosperous future for our great nation.” The post Military kills 11 terrorists, arrests 22, rescues 25 kidnapped victims in one week appeared first on Vanguard News .

Over 340 children killed in Gaza since ceasefire, says Unicef
items.description: UNITED NATIONS: More than 340 children have been reportedly killed and hundreds more injured in Gaza since a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel was announced, the UN Children’s Fund (Unicef) said on Friday, warning that children continue to face grave risks despite the truce. “For families mourning the loss of their children , those terrible statistics do not equate with a ceasefire,” Unicef spokesperson Ricardo Pires told reporters in Geneva. The Unicef noted that five boys and two girls had been reported killed in Gaza over the preceding two weeks, while at least 33 children were seriously injured in air strikes, drone strikes and gunfire across the territory. Two other boys died from injuries sustained earlier, Pires said. Around 800,000 children remain displaced, most living in tents or damaged buildings, while an estimated 60,000 have lost one or both parents during the war or since the ceasefire, according to the Unicef. Nearly every child needs some form of mental health support to recover from the effects of the conflict. The agency called on the parties to the conflict to uphold the ceasefire, comply with UN Security Council Resolution 2803 and meet their obligations under international humanitarian law. “Above all, we need to listen to the voices of children in Gaza,” the Unicef said, stressing that recovery meant more than survival. Children needed to return to school, spend time with friends and family, have dignified shelter, play safely and receive healthcare, the agency said. “Gaza’s children have suffered far too much, for far too long,” it added. The agency stressed the need to maintain an uninterrupted flow of humanitarian and commercial supplies into Gaza, following reports that private traders had halted cooperation with Israeli authorities over the entry of commercial trucks carrying food. Pires recalled that supplies had been unable to enter Gaza before the ceasefire, when famine was declared by UN-backed food security experts. “We can’t go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods and services that they require,” he said. Despite the continuing hardship, Unicef has helped more than 560,000 children return to learning since the ceasefire, including through more than 200 learning centres it supports. The agency has also provided digital cash assistance to more than 380,000 people and safe water to 1.2 million people.

items.title: Trump signs executive order waiving new Russia sanctions, tariffs
items.description: President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia’s energy revenues after signing them into law last month. The Lindsey Graham Act — named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill — allowed Trump the authority to impose duties up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. “As described further in section 4 of this order, I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” the executive order said. The law targeted Russia’s energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions. Trump’s reversal on the Russia sanctions comes in after a controversial deal he struck with Putin that would allow Russia diesel exports in exchange for US sanctions relief. Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since the deal, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calling it a “weak decision” and Ukrainian forces resuming attacks on Russian oil refineries. items.title: Drug Addiction: Arrest is not recovery – Prof Daniel Ikpechukwu
items.description: *Why Nigeria must connect accountability for drug-related offences with access to treatment, rehabilitation and sustained support for young people By Sola Ogundipe At the 4th Vanguard Mental Health Summit, Prof Daniel Ikpechukwu, US-based addiction and behavioural health specialist, substance-use counsellor and psychology educator who focuses on addiction treatment, behavioural health and rehabilitation, challenges Nigerian authorities to bridge the gap between drug enforcement, treatment and recovery Punished but not healed A 22-year-old is arrested after repeated drug-related offences. He is prosecuted, taken into custody and eventually released. But the addiction that may have contributed to his behaviour remains untreated. He returns to the same pressures, the same environment and, potentially, the same pattern of drug use and offending. Soon, he is back in trouble. What has the justice system achieved? It has processed an offender, imposed a consequence and completed its immediate task. But if the underlying problem remains unaddressed, the young man may return to the same cycle, with another arrest, another court appearance and another family crisis waiting around the corner. Consider a different possibility. At the first point of contact with the justice system, the young man is screened for substance use problems, assessed by qualified professionals and held accountable in a way that also addresses his treatment needs. Where the law permits and the circumstances justify it, he is referred to appropriate treatment, supported through recovery and helped to rebuild his life. The difference between the two pathways could be the difference between repeated contact with the justice system and a genuine opportunity to recover. For Nigeria, where millions of people have been estimated to use psychoactive substances, the question is no longer simply how to punish drug-related offending. It is whether the country is doing enough to prevent addiction from becoming a revolving door through its police stations, courts and correctional facilities. This was the central challenge raised by Dr Daniel Ikpechukwu, a behavioural psychologist and addiction specialist, in his presentation, Youth Drug Addiction and the Justice System: Advancing Treatment, Rehabilitation and Recovery in Nigeria, at the fourth Vanguard Mental Health Summit in Lagos. Ikpechukwu’s argument was neither that drug-related offences should be excused nor that addiction should automatically shield anyone from the consequences of crime. Rather, Nigeria needs a justice response that recognises the distinction between criminal accountability and the clinical needs of a person whose substance use may be contributing to repeated offending. Nigeria’s revolving door of arrest, release and relapse According to Ikpechukwu, drug use does not occur in isolation. For many young people, it intersects with unemployment, economic pressure, trauma, peer influence, family stress and social exclusion. In his presentation, Ikpechukwu’s argument brought the intersection of public health and justice into focus. A young person’s encounter with the justice system, he showed, can become either a revolving door of arrest, release and repeat offending or a turning point towards assessment, treatment and recovery. He challenged the country to rethink its response to youth drug addiction and the intersection between substance use disorders and the criminal justice system. In his presentation, Ikpechukwu posed a question that went to the heart of the debate: “Which pathway better protects the young person, the family and society?” His argument was not that drug-related offences should be excused or that addiction should become a blanket defence against criminal responsibility. Rather, he called for a response that recognises the distinction between criminal accountability and the treatment of a health condition. “Not excusing crime. Not criminalising illness. Not abandoning accountability,” Ikpeachukwu stressed in framing the purpose of a more effective response. The goal, he explained, should be to “identify addiction early”, “assess risk and need”, “hold people accountable”, “treat what is treatable” and “support recovery”. His words “Not every person who uses drugs has an addiction..Not every offence committed by a person who uses drugs is caused by addiction.” For Nigeria, where drug use and the consequences of substance use disorders remain significant public health concerns, he explained that this distinction has implications for the police, courts, correctional institutions, health authorities and agencies responsible for drug control. It also raises a difficult question about what happens after enforcement: when a young person is identified as needing help, is appropriate treatment available, and who ensures that the person can access it? Price of treating illness as crime Ikpechukwu asked: ‘Do we wait for addiction to become a crime problem before treating it as a health problem?” The question resonates with public health and drug prevention messaging associated with the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA). The scale of the challenge was underscored by the UNIDOC’s national drug-use survey, conducted in 2018 and published in 2019. The survey estimated that 14.3 million Nigerians aged 15 to 64 had used drugs in the previous year. About one in five people who used drugs had a drug use disorder, while nearly 40 per cent of high-risk drug users who wanted treatment were unable to obtain it. “These are historical estimates rather than current prevalence figures, but they point to a longstanding concern: the gap between the need for treatment and access to care.” For young people, he noted, substance use may intersect with trauma, family strain, unemployment, economic pressure, peer influence and social exclusion, but these circumstances do not excuse offending, but they can complicate recovery. “Where services are scarce, treatment is unaffordable or follow-up support is weak, a young person may leave custody without the care needed to sustain recovery or the practical support needed to rebuild a life.” Ikpechukwu’s presentation challenged authorities to look beyond arrests and prosecutions and ask whether the system is producing better outcomes. Who ensures that a young person referred for treatment actually receives it? What happens when rehabilitation is recommended but suitable services are unavailable? Who follows up after release to determine whether treatment continues and whether the individual is reintegrating into the community? In his view, these responsibilities cannot rest on law enforcement alone, they require coordination among health authorities, justice institutions, drug-control agencies, qualified treatment providers, families and communities. They also require clear measures of progress, including access to treatment, completion of appropriate programmes, continuity of care after release, successful reintegration and reductions in repeat offending. “Treatment itself must be more than a referral or a court order. Where clinically appropriate and legally permissible, it should involve proper assessment, medical and psychological care, relapse prevention and continuing support. “Depending on the individual’s circumstances, recovery may also require help returning to education, developing employable skills, securing work and rebuilding damaged family relationships.” Ikpechukwu cautioned against treating rehabilitation as a box-ticking exercise. His warning was direct: “Mandate treatment carefully. Never mandate poor treatment. A court order cannot create treatment facilities where none exist, guarantee qualified care or ensure that support continues after release.” Any diversion or treatment programme must therefore be based on clinical need, lawful criteria, due process and appropriate safeguards, while protecting public safety. “Ultimately, the issue is not whether Nigeria should choose treatment over accountability. It is whether the country can make both work together, responding firmly to offending while ensuring that young people who need treatment are not left without help.” When youth addiction becomes a justice problem As he put it, “The measure of success is not simply fewer arrests, it is fewer young people trapped in addiction, crisis and repeat offending.” That requires authorities to measure not only how many people are arrested or prosecuted, but also whether those who need care can obtain it, whether treatment continues after release and whether young people have a realistic chance of returning to their families and communities without falling back into the same cycle. His closing message captured the challenge facing Nigeria’s justice and public health systems: “Justice should hold young people accountable, but where addiction is part of the problem, recovery must become part of the solution.” The real test is whether Nigeria can turn that possibility into a functioning system, one in which treatment is accessible, accountability is meaningful and recovery is treated not as an afterthought, but as part of the solution. items.title: Rencontre à l’IRMC à Tunis sur le sionisme, une idéologie coloniale
items.description: L’Institut de recherche sur le Maghreb contemporain ( IRMC ) organise une rencontre-débat autour de l’ouvrage ‘‘Le sionisme, une invention européenne. Genèse d’une idéologie’’ de Sonia Dayan-Herzbrun, professeure émérite de sociologie politique à l’Université Paris-Cité (Lux Editeur, Québec, Canada, 17 octobre 2025, 128 pages), le mardi 20 octobre 2026 à partir de 17h30, en présence de l’auteure de l’ouvrage. Le sionisme, dans ses différentes déclinaisons, est et a toujours été une idéologie coloniale dont on constate aujourd’hui les conséquences effroyables. Ce n’est pas dans la tradition rabbinique mais bien au cœur de la modernité européenne que le sionisme plonge ses racines. Dans l’Occident chrétien, on considérait les diverses communautés de religion juive comme un peuple en exil, originaire d’une terre mythique à la géographie indéterminée. Jusqu’à l’ère moderne, la relation à ce lieu est restée pour les Juifs essentiellement symbolique, voire mystique. Ce n’est qu’à la fin du XIX e siècle qu’elle cherchera à s’ancrer dans une réalité géographique et politique, sous l’impulsion de ce qu’on appelle le «sionisme chrétien» . Une forme de messianisme se combine alors au projet de colonisation de la Palestine et d’expansion de l’Empire britannique. Répondant aux attentes du sionisme chrétien, le sionisme politique de Theodor Herzl et de ses successeurs s’inscrit au confluent de plusieurs courants d’idées très présents en Europe entre le XIX e et le XX e siècle : les nationalismes, les utopies coloniales et l’orientalisme. L’unité de la nation se fait autour d’un récit qui transforme la Bible en livre historique fiable et nie le passé de la terre sur lequel il est censé se dérouler. Toutes les manipulations politiques deviennent alors possibles jusqu’à l’instauration de l’Etat d’Israël, son expansion par l’expropriation violente des terres des Palestiniens et les interminables guerres contre ses voisins au Proche-Orient : Egypte, Liban, Syrie et jusqu’en Iran. Cet expansionnisme est illustré par concept géopolitique et religieux du Grand Israël ( Eretz Yisrael HaShlema , en hébreu) qui désigne l’extension de l’État d’Israël sur l’ensemble de ses supposées frontières bibliques, la fameuse «Terre promise» décrite dans la Bible et qui s’étendrait du Nil à l’Euphrate, c’est-à-dire de l’Egypte à l’Irak. Ce concept colonialiste, illustré par le drapeau même d’Israël (où les deux traits bleus symbolisent les deux fleuves), fonde la politique belliqueuse et expansionniste du gouvernement d’extrême-droite actuel en Israël, conduit par le Premier ministre Benjamin Netanyahu. Prennent part à la discussion de l’ouvrage : Amin Allal, chercheur en science politique (IRMC), et Adrien Thibault, chercheur en sociologie et science politique (IRMC). I. B. L’article Rencontre à l’IRMC à Tunis sur le sionisme, une idéologie coloniale est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .
