Bettina Heinen-Ayech, une œuvre marquée par la lumière et les paysages de la Tunisie
items.description: Du 23 au 25 octobre 2026, à l’occasion de son 30 e anniversaire, la foire internationale d’art ARTfair Innsbruck, en Autriche, rendra hommage à la peintre Bettina Heinen-Ayech (1937–2020), artiste germano-algérienne dont l’œuvre fut profondément marquée par la lumière et les paysages de la Tunisie. Installée dès 1963 à Guelma, dans l’est de l’Algérie, à proximité de la frontière tunisienne, Bettina Heinen-Ayech entretint pendant près de six décennies une relation particulièrement étroite avec la Tunisie. Elle parcourut régulièrement le pays, peignant ses paysages, ses villes historiques, ses villages et ses habitants. De Tabarka à Tunis et Carthage, de Nabeul à Kairouan, d’El-Djem à Gafsa, elle trouva dans la diversité des paysages tunisiens une source d’inspiration constante. L’exposition internationale d’Innsbruck constitue aujourd’hui une nouvelle reconnaissance majeure pour cette artiste qui consacra l’essentiel de sa vie à la peinture et dont la Tunisie occupa une place importante dans l’univers artistique et personnel. Une relation privilégiée avec la Tunisie depuis 1963 En février 1963, quelques mois après l’indépendance de l’Algérie, Bettina Heinen-Ayech s’installe à Guelma auprès de son époux, Abdelhamid Ayech (1926–2010). La proximité géographique de Guelma avec la Tunisie favorise très rapidement ses voyages dans le pays voisin, qu’elle découvre et apprend à aimer dès cette époque. À partir de 1963, la peintre effectue régulièrement des séjours en Tunisie, parcourant différentes régions avec ses couleurs, ses pinceaux et son matériel de peinture. Ces voyages deviennent une composante durable de son existence et de sa création artistique. La Tunisie lui offre une remarquable diversité de paysages, de lumières et d'atmosphères : le littoral méditerranéen, les montagnes boisées du Nord-Ouest, les anciennes cités, les plaines agricoles, les villages de l’intérieur et les paysages arides du Sud. Elle ne se contente pas de visiter ces lieux. Fidèle à sa pratique de la peinture sur le motif, elle s’y installe pour travailler directement devant la nature, cherchant à saisir les variations de lumière, les couleurs et le caractère particulier de chaque région. Au fil des décennies, cette proximité donne naissance à une œuvre tunisienne importante, témoignage pictural d’un attachement profond au pays. Tabarka : une source d’inspiration particulièrement intense Parmi toutes les régions tunisiennes qu’elle découvre, Tabarka et ses environs occupent une place privilégiée dans son œuvre. Située non loin de Guelma, sur la côte méditerranéenne, cette région devient l’une de ses destinations de prédilection. Bettina Heinen-Ayech y revient régulièrement pour peindre les montagnes verdoyantes, les forêts, les reliefs descendant vers la mer, les villages et les paysages côtiers. Elle est particulièrement sensible à la rencontre entre la végétation luxuriante du Nord-Ouest tunisien et les couleurs changeantes de la Méditerranée. Les contrastes entre les montagnes, les forêts, la mer et la lumière méditerranéenne lui offrent des possibilités picturales qu’elle explore inlassablement. Son travail dans la région de Tabarka s’inscrit ainsi parmi les expressions les plus personnelles de sa relation artistique avec la Tunisie. De Tunis à Carthage, de Kairouan à Gafsa : une peintre à la découverte du pays L’intérêt de Bettina Heinen-Ayech pour la Tunisie ne se limite toutefois pas à la région de Tabarka. Au cours de ses nombreux séjours, elle découvre et peint également Tunis et Carthage, où l’histoire, l’architecture et la lumière méditerranéenne constituent autant de sujets d’inspiration. Elle travaille aussi à Nabeul, sur la péninsule du Cap Bon, région dont les paysages et la vie quotidienne nourrissent son regard de peintre. Dans l’intérieur du pays, elle se rend notamment à Kairouan, ville chargée d’histoire, ainsi qu’à El-Djem, célèbre pour son patrimoine architectural antique. Plus au sud, ses voyages la conduisent jusqu’à Gafsa, où elle découvre d’autres couleurs, d’autres reliefs et des paysages annonçant les régions présahariennes. Ces déplacements témoignent de sa volonté de connaître la Tunisie dans toute sa diversité, bien au-delà des grands centres urbains et des destinations touristiques. Pour elle, chaque région possède une identité propre, une lumière particulière et une atmosphère que la peinture peut exprimer. Ses œuvres tunisiennes constituent ainsi un témoignage artistique de plusieurs décennies de rencontres avec les paysages et la culture du pays. Une artiste également présente dans la vie culturelle tunisienne La relation de Bettina Heinen-Ayech avec la Tunisie ne fut pas uniquement celle d’une peintre voyageuse. Elle exposa à plusieurs reprises ses œuvres à Tunis, participant ainsi à la vie artistique et culturelle de la capitale. Ces expositions lui permirent de présenter sa peinture au public tunisien et de faire connaître son regard personnel sur les paysages de l’Afrique du Nord. Son attachement à la Tunisie s’exprimait également à travers les relations humaines nouées au fil de ses séjours et son intérêt constant pour la culture et les habitants du pays. Pour cette artiste profondément européenne par sa formation, mais dont l’existence fut intimement liée au Maghreb, les frontières nationales ne constituaient pas des frontières artistiques. L’Algérie et la Tunisie formaient deux espaces voisins, différents et complémentaires, qui nourrissaient sa sensibilité et sa création. Sa peinture témoigne ainsi d’une rencontre durable entre les traditions picturales européennes et les paysages de l’Afrique du Nord. Une carrière artistique reconnue sur les deux rives de la Méditerranée Née en Allemagne en 1937, Bettina Heinen-Ayech manifeste très tôt un talent exceptionnel pour la peinture. Formée dans l’environnement artistique de la colonie de peintres de Solingen, elle bénéficie notamment de l’enseignement du peintre Erwin Bowien (1899–1972). Dès sa jeunesse, elle participe à d’importantes expositions en Europe et développe progressivement un langage pictural personnel, caractérisé par une grande liberté de couleur, une sensibilité particulière à la lumière et une approche expressive du paysage. Son installation en Algérie en 1963 marque une étape déterminante de son parcours. Durant près de six décennies, elle peint aussi bien en Afrique du Nord que dans différents pays européens, maintenant un dialogue artistique permanent entre les deux rives de la Méditerranée. En Algérie, son œuvre bénéficie d’une reconnaissance institutionnelle importante. Le Musée national des beaux-arts d’Alger lui consacre notamment deux grandes rétrospectives, en 1993 et 2004, et conserve des œuvres de l’artiste dans ses collections. En 2014, le Musée national public Cirta de Constantine organise une nouvelle grande rétrospective consacrée à son parcours artistique. Elle reçoit également plusieurs distinctions officielles, parmi lesquelles le Grand Prix de la ville d’Alger en 1976, ainsi que des hommages des institutions culturelles algériennes. Mais sa carrière dépasse largement le cadre d’un seul pays. Ses voyages et ses expositions témoignent de l’itinéraire d’une artiste qui a construit une œuvre originale au croisement de plusieurs cultures. La Tunisie, une patrie artistique de cœur Pour Bettina Heinen-Ayech, la Tunisie ne fut jamais une simple destination de voyage. La proximité avec son lieu de résidence à Guelma, la fréquence de ses séjours et les liens humains qu’elle y développa firent de ce pays une partie familière et précieuse de son existence. Elle y revint pendant des décennies, découvrant sans cesse de nouveaux sujets et retrouvant des paysages auxquels elle était profondément attachée. Tabarka, Tunis, Carthage, Nabeul, El-Djem, Kairouan et Gafsa comptent ainsi parmi les lieux qui ont nourri son inspiration. Son œuvre constitue aujourd’hui un témoignage artistique de cette relation particulière avec la Tunisie. Lorsqu’elle s’éteint en 2020, Bettina Heinen-Ayech laisse derrière elle un ensemble pictural considérable qui reflète près de soixante-dix années de création artistique, dont une partie importante est consacrée aux paysages et aux habitants du Maghreb. Reconnaissance internationale pour une artiste géniale Du 23 au 25 octobre 2026, à l’occasion de son trentième anniversaire, la foire internationale ARTfair Innsbruck rendra un hommage exceptionnel à Bettina Heinen-Ayech. Une importante présentation muséale permettra au public international de découvrir un ensemble représentatif de son œuvre, illustrant les différentes étapes de sa carrière. Une attention particulière sera portée à sa peinture inspirée par l’Afrique du Nord, où elle développa un langage pictural personnel, marqué par l’intensité de la lumière méditerranéenne et la diversité des paysages. Cet hommage constitue une nouvelle étape dans la reconnaissance internationale d’une artiste dont l’existence et la création furent profondément marquées par les échanges entre l’Europe et le Maghreb. Pour son fils, Dr Haroun Ayech, qui se consacre aujourd’hui à la sauvegarde et à la transmission de l’héritage artistique de sa mère, cette manifestation possède une signification particulière : «Ma mère entretenait avec la Tunisie une relation très profonde. Dès son installation à Guelma en 1963, elle s’est rendue régulièrement dans ce pays voisin qu’elle aimait beaucoup. Elle y a parcouru et peint de nombreuses régions, avec une prédilection particulière pour Tabarka, mais aussi Tunis, Carthage, Nabeul, Kairouan, El-Djem et Gafsa. La Tunisie faisait véritablement partie de son univers artistique et affectif. Elle y avait ses habitudes, ses souvenirs et de nombreux sujets d’inspiration. Elle était également heureuse d’avoir pu présenter ses œuvres à plusieurs reprises au public tunisien. Voir aujourd’hui sa peinture honorée à l’échelle internationale est pour moi une grande joie. J’y vois également un hommage aux paysages, à la lumière et à la culture de la Tunisie, ce pays auquel ma mère était si profondément attachée.» Une nouvelle grande exposition en Allemagne en 2027 Cette reconnaissance internationale se poursuivra dès le début de l’année prochaine. Du 16 janvier au 4 avril 2027, le Kunstmuseum Schwaan, en Allemagne, consacrera une nouvelle grande exposition à Bettina Heinen-Ayech. Cette manifestation présentera un vaste panorama de sa création, depuis les premières années de sa carrière jusqu’aux œuvres de sa maturité inspirées par les paysages européens et nord-africains. Des œuvres des peintres Erwin Bowien et Amud Uwe Millies, deux autres représentants importants de la colonie artistique de Solingen, compléteront cette présentation. Cette exposition offrira une nouvelle occasion de faire découvrir au public européen le parcours exceptionnel d’une artiste qui fit de la peinture un dialogue permanent entre les cultures, les paysages et les peuples. L’article Bettina Heinen-Ayech, une œuvre marquée par la lumière et les paysages de la Tunisie est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: DSS, military, police arrest 5 over NYSC members kidnap
items.description: …As 3 others escape with gunshot injuries By Soni Daniel Operatives of the Department of State Services (DSS), the military and police have arrested five suspected members of a criminal gang allegedly responsible for the abduction of 20 prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members in Imo State on Nigeria’s 66th Independence Day. Five other suspected members of the gang, however, escaped with gunshot injuries prompting a massive manhunt for them. The suspects were apprehended during a series of intelligence-led operations conducted at different locations in Rivers and Abia States. However, in the course of the operation, three other suspects escaped with varying degrees of injury. Security sources disclosed that the operations were carried out between October 10 and 14 in Port Harcourt, Rivers State and Aba South LGA. Abia State. Recall that 20 NYSC members were abducted by armed men along Owerri–Onitsha Expressway in Imo State on October 1, 2026, as they travelled to their assigned orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states. The victims were subsequently rescued on October 7, 2026, during a joint security operation at Amakohia Ubi Village. The string of operations mark a significant breakthrough in efforts to track down the perpetrators, dismantle the criminal network allegedly responsible for the abduction and bring those involved to justice. A security source described the development as a major relief, noting that security agencies had sustained a wide-ranging manhunt for the abductors. “This is a huge sigh of relief. Security agencies have been on a manhunt for the abductors, and we are elated that they have been captured. We strongly believe they will be charged to Court by DSS and the corps members will get justice,” the source said. The post DSS, military, police arrest 5 over NYSC members kidnap appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: NFF Normalisation Committee: FIFA keeps Nigeria waiting
items.description: The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) is still awaiting clarification from FIFA following Thursday’s FIFA Council meeting in Zurich, Switzerland, amid expectations that the country’s football leadership crisis would be on the front burner. The FIFA Council held its 37th meeting on October 15, 2026, with discussions covering football development funding, governance reforms and disciplinary procedures. However, FIFA’s published statement on the meeting did not confirm whether the Council approved the proposed Normalisation Committee for Nigeria. The absence of a public announcement does not necessarily mean Nigeria’s situation was not discussed behind closed doors. Among the key developments, FIFA announced plans to increase football development investment to US$6.35 billion for the 2027–2030 cycle, covering its 211 member associations, confederations and other stakeholders. The proposed framework could allow individual member associations to receive allocations of up to US$25 million, subject to applicable requirements and approval procedures. The Council also agreed to establish a working group to examine FIFA’s governance framework and directed relevant committees to review disciplinary procedures. The meeting attracted particular interest in Nigeria following the August resignations of former NFF President Ibrahim Gusau, General Secretary Mohammed Sanusi and members of the federation’s executive board. A joint FIFA and Confederation of African Football (CAF) delegation subsequently visited Nigeria in September to consult stakeholders and examine possible solutions to the crisis. One option reportedly under consideration is a Normalisation Committee to manage the federation temporarily, implement reforms and organise elections. Earlier reports indicated that the matter could be considered under the FIFA Council’s miscellaneous agenda. On Thursday October 15, Nigerian football stakeholders waited in vain for official clarification on whether FIFA will constitute a Normalisation Committee and issue a timetable for restoring elected leadership. But neither of these happened as at press time. The post NFF Normalisation Committee: FIFA keeps Nigeria waiting appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ‘I’ve intercepted 573 Benue girls from traffickers, returned over 103 from outside Nigeria since March’ — Acrivist Yaaya
items.description: By Peter Duru, Makurdi At 36, Sughnen Yaaya has taken on what many would consider a dangerous and daunting task of confronting the menace of human trafficking in Benue, a state he says has recorded the highest cases of trafficking in the country. Yaaya, an activist and anti-human trafficking campaigner, has, since March 2026, been involved in the interception of hundreds of young girls allegedly being trafficked within Nigeria, while also coordinating the rescue and return of victims from countries like Ghana, Mali, Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina Faso among others. He says he has so far intercepted 573 Benue girls within Nigeria and facilitated the return of 103 others from outside the country. He also claims that about 32 Benue girls have died in foreign countries in circumstances linked to trafficking. In this interview, Yaaya spoke on what motivated his intervention, how the trafficking networks operate, the challenges he has encountered, alleged attempts by traffickers to intimidate him, his collaboration with security agencies and the need for stronger measures to combat trafficking. Excerpt: How old are you, because you look so young and you have taken up a task that is quite herculean? I am 36 years old. At 36, why did you choose to lead an anti-trafficking campaign, what is the motivation? If you check everywhere, over time, there have been issues of insecurity and other challenges in Benue. Notwithstanding the hardship, some people have now resorted to trafficking, perhaps for profit-making and other reasons. From the available data, Benue is the state with the highest number of human trafficking cases. So, as a citizen of Benue state, I thought it was wise to see if I could help. I decided to campaign and create awareness so that people would know that this is happening. Aside from my inability to provide solutions to insecurity, kidnapping and other challenges, I chose to fight human trafficking and organise anti-human trafficking campaigns. I don’t have any other motive. It is not for profit-making. I am just trying to help in my little way. In the course of your voluntary work, how many people have you rescued since the beginning of this year? My brother, they are many. Let me break it down for you. From March till now, I don’t like giving out my data because I work with people. I work with the police, and if I have to give out any data, I think it would be wise to go through the proper channels. But, since this is for a report, let me say that from March till now, I have intercepted 573 girls. By interception, I mean that we stopped them before they were taken out of the country. We could intercept them at a motor park or somewhere along the route because I have people who assist me. We have intercepted 573 girls from March till now. These are girls intercepted within Nigeria, especially in Lagos. And these were all Benue girls? Yes, all of them were Benue girls. I don’t have the resources to focus on people from other states. I am focused on Benue. For those we rescued outside the country and brought back home, the number is 103. You rescued them from outside the country? Yes. Some were rescued from Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina Faso and other countries. Outside the country, I have people who assist me. In one particular Nigerian embassy, I have a Benue brother who helps me. Once I give him the location, he mobilises, goes there and helps rescue them. So, apart from those rescued outside the country, the ones you intercepted inside Nigeria are over 500? Yes, those within Nigeria are interceptions If you intercept them, that means traffickers couldn’t get them outside the country? Exactly. That is the essence of interception. This whole thing is also happening within Nigeria. For instance, in Benin, Edo and others states there are places where women and young girls are allegedly kept for prostitution. And they are all Benue girls? Yes, they are all Benue girls, like I said. All Benue girls. I have videos and pictures. If you want, I can forward them to you. I have many pictures. We also have about 32 who died outside the country. If you go through my social media handles, you will see that I sometimes post about Benue girls dying in Ghana. And this record is from March 2026 till now? Yes, just from March. That was when I started taking the issue seriously. Are you getting any support from the government? No, no single support. So, you are doing this from your pocket? From my pocket. I also have some brothers who support me. Sometimes, people who follow me on social media and see what I am doing send me messages saying they want to help. The highest support I have received so far is N500,000. I have received N500,000, N200,000, N100,000, N10,000 and so on from individuals. What are the challenges you have been facing in the course of your intervention? There are a lot of challenges. First, the traffickers and their families try to come after me and my family. That is one major challenge. Some of them even use security agencies. As I speak, there’s a petition written against me by a trafficker in Lagos. According to her, she trafficked only three girls. But those girls told me that she took six of them to Ghana. When I contacted her, she said she took only three and brought back two, meaning that only one is still there. When I asked her to send the remaining girl back home, she went and wrote a petition against me at Zone 2 in Lagos. In Nigeria, if you have money, you can do almost anything. That is one of the challenges. Finance is another major challenge, and it is the biggest one. If I am well-funded, I think I can expand my work. There are victims from other states who have been contacting me. Last week, some girls from Rivers State called me from Mali for assistance. For now, I want to focus on Benue because of some limitations and other factors. But if I have the money, why not expand the work to other states? I will. Human trafficking is a major challenge in Nigeria, and Benue is currently topping the list, according to the data available to us. How many of the traffickers have you been able to get arrested in the course of this intervention? They are many. When it comes to arrests, I really appreciate the Benue State Police Command for the wonderful job it is doing. Initially, I was working with the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons, NAPTIP, but I moved from NAPTIP to the police in March. That is why I gave you the statistics starting from March. The number of people arrested and remanded awaiting trial is now 59. When I arrest some of them, I sometimes give them a soft landing. That is if they bring the victims back, take them to the hospital and perhaps empower them. Some of them comply and I let the matter go. Given the inherent dangers in this assignment, are you not scared for your life? Of course I am very scared. I count my days every day. But I know that when you are doing what is right, God is always there for you. What I am doing is to help the society, especially the underprivileged. So, I am not really scared in the true sense of the word. Do you have personal security? I don’t have the money for that for now. God is my security. When I have the money, I can get security personnel attached to me. But for now, I am doing the work and praying to God for protection. Is the Benue State Government assisting you? No, not at all. But I get assistance from Benue Links, the state-owned transport company, which helps to transport some of the girls back home when we rescue them. What is your final word to young girls and traffickers out there? My message to the traffickers is that we are getting closer to the end of the war against human trafficking. If they still want to move more people, we will enforce more measures against them. If I have what it takes, I believe you won’t see anything like human trafficking again. But I have developed strategies over time. I have developed major strategies, including working with immigration officials, people at the borders and others. If we can close all the leakages, I think we will achieve good results. For my sisters, I am always advising them to stay at home, go to school and get educated. If you are travelling as an educated person, you should know that you need a passport and all the necessary documents before travelling. If somebody says they are offering you a job, you should be able to check the company’s website and verify everything. Make your findings very well before travelling. I advise them to stay safe, get educated and become useful to themselves. items.title: 2027: ‘I won’t restore petrol subsidy’ — YPP candidate Agada
items.description: The presidential candidate of the Young Progressives Party (YPP), Peter Agada, has ruled out restoring petrol subsidy if elected president in the 2027 general elections, saying he would retain the policy introduced by President Bola Tinubu. Agada made this known on Friday during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today , where he outlined his approach to addressing Nigeria’s revenue and expenditure challenges. Tinubu announced the removal of petrol subsidy during his inauguration on May 29, 2023, a decision that led to higher petrol prices and increased the cost of goods and services. While some presidential hopefuls, including African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidate Atiku Abubakar, have advocated restoring the subsidy to reduce fuel costs and ease economic hardship, Agada said his administration would maintain its removal. “I will stick to the gun with the present administration. We will remove subsidy the way they have done,” he said. The YPP candidate argued that Nigeria’s economic challenges were not solely a consequence of subsidy removal but were also linked to how the country manages oil revenues and the expenses incurred in producing crude oil. Citing remarks by the Minister of State for Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, Agada questioned how much revenue the Federal Government actually retains from crude oil production after royalties and other deductions. He argued that the amount left for the government was insufficient to meet the country’s needs, despite its oil production capacity. Agada said his administration would scrutinise the Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) system to identify waste and improve government revenue. “We want to interrogate that system because we think that the wastage and majority of the challenges Nigeria is facing in terms of lower revenue is coming from that whole regime or that system that Nigeria practices,” he said. He maintained that the system had been faulty from its inception and required reforms to address inefficiencies. Agada acknowledged that Nigeria faced both revenue and expenditure problems but said excessive or inefficient spending was the more pressing concern. He argued that improving public expenditure management and plugging leakages would be central to addressing the country’s economic difficulties without reversing the petrol subsidy removal policy. items.title: Suspended Anglican Archbishop Ibezim, sues Church Primate
items.description: By Vincent Ujumadu AWKA — The Anglican Archbishop of the Province of the Niger and Bishop of the Diocese of Awka, Most Rev. Alexander Ibezim, has instituted legal proceedings against the Primate of the Church of Nigeria, Most Rev. Henry C. Ndukuba, challenging his alleged suspension and moves to subject him to disciplinary proceedings. In an originating summons filed at the High Court of Anambra State, Awka Judicial Division, Ibezim is seeking the interpretation of relevant provisions of the 2020 Constitution and Canons of the Church of Nigeria (Anglican Communion) governing disciplinary proceedings against serving diocesan bishops. Ndukuba is listed as the first defendant, while the Dean of the Church of Nigeria, Most Rev. Blessing Enyindah, who chaired a visitation team to the Diocese of Awka, is the second defendant. The suit challenges the legality of the visitation team, which Ibezim described as “illegally constituted” by the Primate in a letter dated June 17, 2026. The archbishop is asking the court to determine the procedure for disciplining a serving diocesan bishop and the extent to which the church’s governing laws must be observed before any sanction can be imposed. Specifically, Ibezim is seeking a declaration that the procedure for disciplining a serving diocesan bishop is provided for under sections 55 and 75 to 76 of the church’s 2020 Constitution, as well as sections 22 to 28 of Canon XVI. He wants the court to affirm that the prescribed procedure must be strictly followed before any disciplinary measure, including suspension or removal from office as Bishop of Awka and Archbishop of the Province of the Niger, can be imposed on him. The claimant is also seeking a declaration that at least one of the 10 offences listed under section 1 of Canon XVI must be established before disciplinary action can lawfully be taken against him. The provisions outline offences for which senior clerics, including the Primate, archbishops, bishops, priests and deacons, may be tried under the church’s disciplinary framework. Ibezim is further asking the court to determine the proper interpretation and application of several constitutional and canonical provisions governing the duties, powers and responsibilities of various offices within the Church of Nigeria. The provisions cited in the suit span Canons V, VI, VII, IX, XII, XIV, XV, XVI and XVII, reflecting the range of legal questions the claimant wants the court to resolve. The defendants, whose address is given as St Matthias House, Plot 942, Ibrahim Waziri Crescent, Gudu District, Apo, Abuja, have 42 days from the date of service of the originating summons to enter an appearance. Recall that in a letter dated October 13, 2026, Ndukuba conveyed the Church of Nigeria’s decision directing Ibezim to proceed on six months’ compulsory leave pending the conclusion of investigations into allegations involving the archbishop and the diocese. items.title: 2027: How to stop election results manipulation — Agbakoba
items.description: •Says, political parties don’t need to depend on INEC alone to produce evidence in court •INEC can declare, but Nigerians can publish authenticated results •If you can’t monitor results, you shouldn’t be on the ballot By Kayode Matthew Before the 2023 general elections were held, the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, boasted that electronic transmission of election results from the polling units to the INEC Result Viewing Portal, IReV, was going to be a game changer. But despite the colossal amount that was invested in it, the game changer failed to change the game with the resultant technical glitches that truncated the process which INEC has been unable to explain till date. We are now three months away from another general election, fixed for January 2027. Election fever does not appear to have gripped the populace. The billboards across the country are yearning for the candidates’ posters. The political parties are yet to hit the streets with their campaigns. What we have are reports of political elites threatening their opponents and residents alike with fire and brimstone. The electoral umpire, on its part, has been trying to keep faith with the schedule of activities on the election timetable even with the spirit of 2023 technical glitches still hovering over its head. However, there are indications that we are going to witness interesting times in the next election. According to an English proverb, once bitten, twice shy. The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, in the 2027 election, Mr Peter Obi contested the 2023 presidential election under the platform of the Labour Party. He is still claiming he won that election but his mandate was stolen when INEC abandoned electronic transmission of results midway and opted for manual collation. This time around, some opposition parties said they would set up an independent system to transmit results from polling units to their situation rooms which would operate alongside INEC’s official transmission process to ensure that votes counted and recorded at polling units were accurately transmitted. Against the background of plans by political parties to set up situation rooms to collate results that have been announced by electoral officials at the polling units, the INEC has therefore warned media organisations not to publish privately collated election results. INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, gave the warning on Thursday September 24, 2026 while speaking at the 24th All Nigeria Editors Conference (ANEC 2026), organised by the Nigerian Guild of Editors in Enugu. He said the media should resist the temptation to publish election results generated by political actors or other private organisations before the commission makes official declarations. The INEC chairman repeated the warning on Tuesday, October 6, 2026 in Abuja at a national stakeholders’ meeting convened to mark 100 days to the 2027 general election arguing that under the Electoral Act, the authority to declare results rests exclusively with the commission. The commission’s warning has therefore provoked reactions from Nigerians who expect their votes to count during the election and look forward to the commission to conduct credible, transparent and fair general elections. Meeting this expectation therefore requires the establishment of transparent processes through which they can independently examine electoral records. In a letter dated October 12, 2026 addressed to the INEC chairman, the former president of the Nigerian Bar Association, NBA, Dr Olisa Agbakoba, SAN, said the commission’s exclusive authority to declare election results formally should not be interpreted as a restriction on the public’s right to report results already announced at polling units or contained in authentic electoral records. Dr Agbakoba drew a distinction between declaration of final election results by INEC and announcement of preliminary results by media organisations. According to him, “While INEC retains its exclusive statutory responsibility for the formal declaration of results, nothing in that responsibility should be understood as prohibiting citizens or the media from reporting results that have been publicly announced at polling units or from publishing information contained in authentic INEC electoral records (Forms EC8A – EC8E), provided that such reporting is accurate and does not misrepresent the official records. “Where polling-unit result sheets are uploaded and made accessible through IReV, citizens, journalists, political parties and observers can view those records, assess them and communicate their contents accurately, while clearly identifying the source and status of the information”. He argued that Section 25 of the Electoral Act, 2026, which governs the relevant functions of electoral officers, must be read alongside other applicable provisions of the Act and “Section 39(1) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, as amended, which guarantees the right to freedom of expression, including the freedom to hold opinions and to receive and impart ideas and information without interference. This constitutional protection is central to the question of whether citizens and the media may communicate information about electoral results that are already publicly available”. Dr Agbakoba then cited the 1984 judgment delivered by Justice Candide Johnson of the High Court of Lagos State in a case between the Nigeria Union of Journalists and the Inspector General of Police where the court declared as unlawful and unconstitutional, the directive by Federal Electoral Commission, FEDECO, (now INEC) warning the media not to publish election results that had not been officially released by it. He therefore urged the Commission to understand the clear distinction between the formal declaration of results and the lawful publication or projection of electoral outcomes based on verifiable records and guarantee the citizens and the media the right to publish and analyse election results from authentic polling unit records ahead of the 2027 general elections. Dr Agbakoba also appeared on Arise News television programme, The Morning Show, last Wednesday to share his perspective on INEC’s warning against the media or the citizens publishing election results. During the programme, he was asked how the public can ensure accuracy of the results announced by the citizens which are already in the public domain and if he intended to take any consequential steps to defend his position. His response: “No, I don’t intend to take any consequential steps because already in 1984, Mr Justice Candide Johnson, in the case concerning NUJ and FEDECO, (now INEC), decided exactly what I’m saying; that journalists have a right to publish results. I think the confusion is that we confuse the declaration of results. That’s the only power that INEC has exclusively, to declare the results. But as you know, the electoral record in terms of voting goes from the polling unit to the ward, to the local government, to the state, to the national collation and to the final announcement. That is the process. If I’m standing at the polling unit and the presiding officer reads the results, I can broadcast it because he has read it. And I can tell you that political parties are going to set up AI processes whereby they’ll be able to pick results from the IReV, because the IReV is simply a compilation of all the results coming from the polling units. “So, this time I predict we’re going to see speed. But the question is whether I’m holding all the results in my hand, authenticated, because Section 124 of the Act warns against publishing fake results and prescribes punishment for it. So, that tells us that if the Act anticipates that you can publish a fake result, it also means that you can publish the results. The real confusion is the doctrinal problem of what INEC can do, which is simply to declare the results. The fact that I have announced the result doesn’t mean that, that is the result. “Remember that even with the famous 1993 free and fairest election in Nigeria, there was no declaration. It was on the board that people saw the results that had been written and it was from there that it was projected that Abiola won. There’s no question that the media, particularly, are entitled to publish results. In any event, the matter has been decided which has not been appealed, and the case is NUJ versus FEDECO, now INEC. And I think that is the decision that binds everybody including INEC. How people trust AI-generated election results “It’s up to the citizens if they wish to set up an AI collation process. The only restriction is that you must publish the results based on what the IReV has set. That’s all. You must source your results. You must say, ‘based on IReV, I hereby project this candidate as the winner of the election. You cannot say, ‘I’m projecting this candidate as a winner’ without attributing it. There must be attribution. If you watch international media, when CNN projected Obama, it went to the board and said, ‘we project Obama as the winner based on the outcomes’. The key here is that you can’t go on a frolic of your own and say, ‘here are the results.’ The results must be results obtained from the process, and the INEC has a source of information flowing from form EC8A up to EC8E. Admissibility of IReV results in court There have been arguments that the Electoral Act should be revisited on the ground that since IReV can be used to authenticate results based on what has been taken from different polling units, should it then not be admissible as evidence in court for post-election matters? Agbakoba agreed with this proposition and went ahead to blame political parties for being lazy in the prosecution of their post-election cases “You’re absolutely right. And here, let me just say political parties have been very lazy. What they do is, they go to court, apply to the justices and say, ‘INEC, can you please release the results?’ But you have the results. Don’t forget that you have party agents that signed EC8A at the polling units. So any political party that is unable to monitor its results is not qualified to be on the ballot. It is your responsibility by law to have polling agents putting your results together. So, when these parties go to court and say, ‘My Lord, can I have results from INEC?’ I think it’s lazy. We ought not to depend only on INEC. So, this point about being able to publish and announce results can be stretched to the issue of proving cases in court”. At this point, one of the anchors of the programme, Mr Rufai Oseni was overwhelmed by Dr Agbakoba’s submissions and poured encomiums on him. He said, “Dr Agbakoba, God bless you, and I say this ad infinitum, God bless you a million times. Because what you have just done is to provide clarity and shame the devil. You have no idea what you have done today, sir. I’m sorry I’ve been theatrical. You see, it’s because people are criminals, that’s why they will never accept the thoughts you are putting forward. They’re criminal in nature and I’ll tell you why. The reason why they keep saying the onus falls on INEC to declare the results is because of their criminal intent of changing the results with INEC. “We saw what happened in Rivers State, that somebody won on the IReV, but what was announced by INEC was different. In the case of America you are talking about, CNN does not even have IReV, they project the result with the exit polls, which is not even an accurate measurement like our own live results. We even have a portal where we have live results but they project with exit polls. So when people say we can’t publish the result, it’s a criminal mindset, and it’s because we have allowed this criminality to continue. INEC wants to be the arbiter, that’s why they’re doing this. My question for you is, how can we stop this level of criminality, that when people win on IReV, INEC would declare something else and say this is what we declared. How to stop the level of criminality In his response, Agbakoba said, “These political parties, I don’t know what’s wrong with them. I don’t know whether they even read the Electoral Act. They have a lot of responsibilities to be able to challenge INEC’s results. But what then happens is that everyone is waiting for INEC to deliver trucks and trucks of results. What you just said is absolutely correct. If the political parties have structures and they are spread around all the polling units, they should be able to, in a matter of hours, have authenticated results. So they don’t need to depend on INEC in court. All they need to show is, here are the results produced from the portals of INEC. I don’t see that a court will say no. But in all of the presidential petitions, this has never been done. Now that I hear that some political parties are organizing to do this, I’m just hoping that that will happen. But the big thing is this; if INEC knows it’s being watched, it will be careful. It will know that somebody is putting together an alternative credible result from the same INEC source. And I hope that would make INEC to be a lot more credible, to deliver what is accurate and not to create what you call criminal results. So we’re hoping that 2027 will be the departure from the past”. Political parties’ lack of structure There are also arguments that many political parties may be unable to challenge whatever result INEC has declared for lack of capacity as some of the parties won’t be able to even recruit enough polling agents. According to the former NBA president, “If you stand for an election on the platform of a particular party for the presidency and you don’t have the structure, then why are you on the ballot? You must have the structures to defend your mandate, which includes the results. So any party that does not have the capacity to even gather its results, that’s its problem. Then you go and depend on INEC’s results and you will have no reason to question the presumption of regularity. But if the party that has the equipment and the wherewithal to have its electoral records intact, present it to the court, then the presumption of regularity that flows in favor of INEC is rebuttable. The court will say, “Oh, we can see something else that is coming from the same source.” So the bottom line is, parties need to be prepared. If you’re not ready to monitor the elections right across Nigeria, don’t go on the ballot or don’t complain. Vanguard News The post 2027: How to stop election results manipulation — Agbakoba appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ‘Raising concerns early part of accountability in workplace’ — Mide-Ibrahim
items.description: By Ayo Taiwo Much of Oluwatobiloba Mide-Ibrahim’s management work comes down to two things: reviewing financial work and helping people understand the decisions behind the figures. At the Association for Diagnostic and Laboratory Medicine, she oversees the close, the financial statements and the records behind them. At FinServe Pro, where she is Chief Operating Officer, she mentors staff and coordinates work across departments. Those roles put technical review and people management in the same conversation. A preparer has to be able to explain a reconciliation. A supervisor has to spot where more investigation is needed. And when several departments contribute to one service, someone has to own the handoffs and the open questions. In this interview, she talked about how she organizes her teams, what she asks in a review and how leaders should respond when someone raises a problem, along with one practical limit of supervision: keeping people accountable without making the whole team depend on one reviewer. How do you organize your team around close deadlines? I make the work and the review responsibilities clear before the deadline arrives. Staff need to know which schedules depend on other teams and when to flag an exception. In review, I focus on significant judgments and open items, beyond whether a task is marked complete. A realistic schedule leaves time to investigate and correct. The final report should reflect the work that was actually done. What do you focus on in a review conversation? One specific task and the thinking behind it. What result did you expect? What information supported your decision? Where did it get difficult? The conversation should end with a practical next step, like clearer documentation, an extra review or a better explanation of the task. Then I follow up, because people need a chance to apply the feedback in their everyday work. Your COO role spans departments. How do you create accountability when several teams contribute to one service? I define who’s responsible at each handoff and the point at which the next team accepts the work. Staff need to know what information should travel with a request and who resolves an exception. When work stalls, the teams involved should identify the missing decision or information and agree who will fix it. You want staff to raise concerns early. Doesn’t that weaken accountability? Raising a concern is part of being accountable. The person still needs to investigate within their own area and help solve the problem. I separate an honest mistake made while following the process from repeatedly ignoring clear instructions, and I respond to the facts. People need to know what good work looks like, where to get help and which decisions need a second look. How do you avoid redoing everyone’s work in review? I make the preparation standard clear and ask people to explain the significant balances and exceptions. Then my review can focus on judgment calls, changes and open questions. If I keep rebuilding someone’s schedule, I need to ask why. Maybe it’s training, maybe the instructions, maybe the task itself. Leading the close means organizing responsibility and review. If I did all the work myself, the team would depend on one person. Finance can feel remote to the rest of an organization. How do you change that? Start with the activity the department recognizes. Explain which cost changed, why, and what decision follows. Budget and forecast conversations need a shared understanding of the work behind the numbers. If a manager questions a charge, show the calculation and listen to what they bring. The goal is a report clear enough that the manager can take part in the decision. What should managers do when deadlines keep requiring overtime? Look at the recurring workload and what it depends on. Is information arriving late? Is one person doing a task nobody else understands? Is the team fixing the same errors every month? I want the cause before I accept overtime as normal. The team needs enough time for proper review. A deadline that’s only met through constant exhaustion tells you the process isn’t reliable. How do you know whether mentoring is working? Look at the work that comes afterwards. Are reconciliations better supported? Are explanations clearer? Does the person spot an exception and ask for review at the right moment? A finished task tells you more than attendance at a training session. We agree on a starting standard and assess progress over a set period. The supervisor also has to create chances to apply what was learned, because development happens in real work. How has your education shaped the way you lead? My business administration degree gave me a foundation in how organizations work. The MBA added a management perspective, and the Business Analytics Certificate sharpened my focus on data and interpretation. I draw on all three when I review a workflow or explain a financial movement. But a technical answer still has to work for the people using it. Education earns its keep when it helps you define the problem, weigh the evidence and explain the right course of action. How do you help staff see the consequences of a routine error? I connect the entry to the report someone relies on. A coding error can change the explanation a department receives. An entry in the wrong period can distort a budget comparison. I go through the records with the person and show how the error travels to the final report. When people understand the consequence, they recognize a similar problem next time, instead of just learning how to correct one entry. What would you do if a capable employee kept submitting work late? Talk with them about why. Which information arrives late? What’s competing for their time? Where are they waiting on a review or a decision from someone else? A capable person still needs a manageable workload and clear priorities, so I look at the process as well as the individual. We agree on an action and I follow up. If the issue is within their control, I make the expectation clear. If the delay comes from a dependency, someone needs to own fixing it. How do you make a team less dependent on the one person who knows every detail? Document the steps and the reasoning, then let a colleague perform the task with review. The instructions should cover the source records, the decisions and how to handle exceptions. A written procedure alone doesn’t prove someone else understands the work, so I ask the colleague to explain the output and investigate a question. The organization gains continuity, and the original expert gets time back for work that truly needs their judgment. What professional habit do you hope your colleagues take into their own leadership roles? Being ready to explain why. If a balance is reliable, show the evidence. If a process needs to change, describe what failed and how you’d fix it. If the information is incomplete, say what work remains, and be willing to admit it. That habit improves technical review and conversations with management alike. I want colleagues to build confidence by understanding their work, and to know how to ask for review, explain the question and come back with a supported recommendation. items.title: Mahama swears in four envoys, tasks them with attracting investment
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has sworn in four ambassadors, charging them to attract investment, expand trade and create opportunities for Ghanaians abroad as part of the government’s Reset Agenda. The President gave the directive at a swearing-in ceremony at the Jubilee House on Friday, October 16, 2026, urging the envoys to make Ghana’s diplomatic missions more responsive to the country’s economic and development priorities. The newly sworn-in envoys are Nana Antwiwaa Dodoo, assigned to Angola; Louis Kwame Obeng, to Qatar; Evelyn Korantemaa Ofosu-Amable, to Israel; and Jedidiah Reuben Adogla, Ghana’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office in Geneva, Switzerland. President Mahama said Ghana’s missions must play a more active role in identifying investors, helping local businesses access foreign markets and building partnerships that support skills development, research and technology transfer. “Our missions play an important role in identifying investors whose interests align with Ghana’s development priorities, helping Ghanaian businesses enter new markets abroad, and building relationships with institutions that can support skills development, research, and technology transfer,” he said. He said the success of Ghana’s economic diplomacy should be measured by the opportunities and jobs created through international partnerships. The President urged the ambassadors to help Ghana secure greater value from its natural resources by promoting local processing and investment in productive industries. He also called for efficient consular services and stronger support for Ghanaians living abroad, stressing that their welfare must remain a priority for diplomatic missions. President Mahama further highlighted Ghana’s application for partnership with the BRICS countries, saying the initiative was intended to broaden the country’s development partnerships and strengthen cooperation among developing economies. He said closer engagement with BRICS could create opportunities for trade, investment, industrialisation and value addition without undermining Ghana’s relations with its traditional partners. The President also directed Ghana’s new ambassador to Israel, Evelyn Korantemaa Ofosu-Amable, to uphold the country’s position on Palestine. “We recognise the sovereign State of Palestine and support a viable two-state solution in which Israel and Palestine will live side by side in peace and security within internationally recognised and secure borders,” he said. He added that Ghana’s international engagements must uphold international law, protect civilians and respect human dignity. President Mahama urged the four envoys to work closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, adhere to government policy and use public resources responsibly. He reminded them that Article 40 of the 1992 Constitution should guide their conduct in promoting and protecting Ghana’s interests abroad.

items.title: Des déplacés regagnent timidement leurs villages malgré une situation sécuritaire fragile à Masisi

items.title: IShowSpeed partners Obamas to bring Ghana history documentary to cinemas on October 28
items.description: Streaming star IShowSpeed has partnered with Breakwater Studios and Higher Ground Productions to bring The Eyes of Ghana , a documentary about the preservation of Ghana’s cinematic history, to cinemas for a one-night screening on October 28, 2026. The screening will take place at participating cinemas in the United States, including major chains and independent theatres. Dates for screenings in Ghana and the United Kingdom have yet to be announced. The film follows 93-year-old Ghanaian cinematographer Chris Hesse, who served as personal cameraman to Ghana’s first President, Kwame Nkrumah, as he races against time and declining eyesight to preserve and repatriate a collection of more than 1,000 reels of historical footage. The footage documents Ghana’s independence era and the wider African liberation movement of the 1950s and 1960s. The United States of Africa? Presented by @ishowspeedsui, executive produced by @BarackObama and @MichelleObama, and directed by two-time Academy Award winner @bgproudfoot, THE EYES OF GHANA follows the story of Chris Hesse – personal cameraman to the first president of Ghana. https://t.co/RiAeYBK5LK — Higher Ground (@HGMedia) October 15, 2026 According to the film’s synopsis, Hesse secretly moved the negatives to London following the 1966 coup that removed Nkrumah from power, preserving images that might otherwise have been lost. IShowSpeed, whose real name is Darren Watkins Jr., said his visit to Ghana earlier in 2026 deepened his connection to the country and its people. In a statement, he said he was honoured to help bring Hesse’s story to a wider audience. He said learning about the cinematographer’s work had strengthened his appreciation of Ghana’s history and the importance of preserving it for future generations. The streamer has built a global following across streaming and social media platforms, giving the documentary access to audiences beyond traditional film and history circles. Film explores Ghana’s visual history Directed by two-time Academy Award winner Ben Proudfoot, The Eyes of Ghana examines Hesse’s efforts to rescue and return archival footage that captures key moments in Ghana’s history and the struggle for African independence. The documentary also highlights the importance of making historical records accessible to younger generations and preserving the work of African filmmakers. It premiered at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival and later won the Audience Award for Best Documentary Feature at the Hamptons International Film Festival. The film is produced by Breakwater Studios and Higher Ground Productions, with Barack and Michelle Obama among its executive producers. The documentary premiered in Ghana in April 2026 at the National Theatre of Ghana, followed by a screening at the University of Ghana’s Cedi Conference Centre, according to information supplied for this report. It has also featured at international film festivals, including the BFI London Film Festival. Director Ben Proudfoot has expressed hope that the film could be screened free of charge in schools across Ghana, allowing students to engage directly with archival footage of the country’s past. Although the October 28 cinema event is confirmed for participating theatres in the United States, organisers have yet to announce dates for further screenings in Ghana and the United Kingdom. Information on tickets and participating cinemas is available through the film’s official website, The Eyes of Ghana .

items.title: Attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure 'worrying' for outlook: Pakistan finance minister
items.description: Pakistan's finance minister on Saturday told AFP the country had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices due to the Iran war, but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were "worrying" for the country's longer-term economic outlook. In an interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Muhammad Aurangzeb said the South Asian country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.
